title: TIPs: a deep learning-guided proteogenomic framework to expand the landscape of transposable element-derived antigens with immunopeptidomics.
data_url: There is no data deposit. Code only: https://github.com/WgShaoLab/TIPs (MIT licence, 435 KB) and https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18595612 (MIT, a single 309,585-byte file TIPs_code_v0.2.zip, resource type 'Workflow'). Results: 30 unique peptide sequences inside Additional file 2, 13059_2026_4191_MOESM2_ESM.docx (30,089 bytes). Inputs are other groups' raw mass-spectrometry deposits at PRIDE (a public proteomics repository): PXD013649, PXD034772, PXD003790; plus GEO (Gene Expression Omnibus) series GSE80137 (RNA sequencing) and GSE182377 / GSE59820 (ribosome profiling).

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Europe PMC search on the DOI returned exactly 1 hit (PMID 42436584, PMC13440072, open access, licence 'cc by-nc-nd', first published 2026-07-11, hasSuppl Y). I downloaded the full text XML (190,262 bytes) and read the abstract, all 13 Results subsections, Discussion, Conclusions, all 21 Methods subsections and the Data availability statement. I downloaded the Europe PMC supplementary bundle (8,024,429 bytes, 15 files) and extracted the three Word documents myself: 13059_2026_4191_MOESM1_ESM.docx (12,268,962 bytes), MOESM2 (30,089 bytes), MOESM3 (25,096 bytes). I wrote my own Word-table parser and counted every cell. ADDITIONAL FILE 2 is the only file in the whole paper that contains data, and it holds exactly four tables: Table S1 = 13 sample rows, columns Sample / Sample type / Treatment / HLA-A / HLA-B / HLA-C / Dataset, zero blank cells, 3 distinct PRIDE accessions, 4 sample types (melanoma, glioblastoma, lung adenocarcinoma, lung squamous cell carcinoma). Table S2 = 11 data rows, columns Target Protein / Peptide / Charge state / Probability / Spectral Count / Best Allele Rank (%) / TE subfamily / TEclass / SampleTreatment; I counted 9 unique peptide sequences (7 LINE, 2 LTR; IVSAQNLIK and ELIALTQALR each appear twice), lengths 9-10 amino acids, 4 target proteins (LORF2_HUMAN 5 unique peptides, LORF1_HUMAN 2, HERVS71_pol 1, MERVL_pol 1). Table S3 = 23 data rows, columns Peptide / Charge state / Probability / Spectral Count / Best Allele Rank (%) / TE subfamily / Sample / Treatment; 21 unique peptide sequences, lengths 9-13, 5 SVA subfamilies, and every single row comes from one cell line (LNT-229). Table S4 = 16 rows of software names and versions. Total deposited unique peptides: 30 (9 + 21), all of them positives, with no negative examples anywhere. MOESM1 is 10 TIFF images plus figure legends (no tables); MOESM3 is Supplementary Notes 1 and 2 as prose (no tables). I listed the GitHub repository tree (not truncated): 60 entries, all Python / Nextflow pipeline code plus one 352,867-byte overview PNG - there is no data directory and no results file. The Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.18595612 is public, MIT, published 2026-02-10, and contains exactly one 309,585-byte code zip. I queried the PRIDE application programming interface for all three input accessions and summed the file sizes myself: PXD003790 lists 65 files totalling 172,542,596,998 bytes (60 Thermo .raw files plus txt-proteome.rar at 2,393,979,876 bytes and MaxQuantOutput.tar.gz at 485,303,935 bytes); PXD013649 lists 97 files totalling 84,018,210,451 bytes (85 .raw plus eight 'search_*.zip' of 23-60 MB and paper_data.zip at 954,495,630 bytes); PXD034772's first page alone is 100 .raw files totalling 229,776,196,927 bytes. All three are 'PARTIAL' submissions on Q Exactive instruments; PXD013649 and PXD034772 are CC0, PXD003790 is 'EBI terms of use'. I downloaded only the 16,242-byte README.txt from PXD013649 and read its file-to-sample mapping. I confirmed via NCBI esummary that GSE80137 exists (12 samples, TXT and XLSX supplementary) and GSE182377 exists ('smORF atlas', 136 samples, no supplementary listed); GSE59820's file list downloaded fine (ribosome-profiling wig files plus a 380,354,560-byte RAW tar). I downloaded no .raw mass-spectrometry file and no sequencing file.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Every headline number in this paper is paper-text-only, because no file contains it. Specifically unverifiable by me: the '20-fold more TE-derived peptides than NewAnce on average'; the 83.4% versus 83.3% predicted-HLA-binder proportions; the 11 NewAnce peptides versus 187 extra TIPs peptides in sample 0D5P; the 19 of 24 recovered and 488 extra peptides in T1185B; the claim that the TIPs search space was 39% of NewAnce's; the 25.4% of peptides that map to multiple genomic loci; the correlations r = 0.72 (peptide count versus subfamily copy number), r = -0.14 and -0.28 (versus insertion age), and r = 0.94 (predicted hydrophobicity versus retention time); the 26 endogenous-retrovirus peptides from 3,173 intact elements (only 2 of those 26 appear in any table); the 67 whole-proteome TE peptides (42 LINE, 14 LTR, 7 SINE, 4 DNA); the 503 tumour-specific and 318 treatment-induced peptides; the claim that these are about 30% of the whole TE immunopeptidome versus under 0.1% of canonical peptides (which would imply roughly 2,700 TE peptides in total, a number the paper never states); the 22 antigens shared across patients; the fragment-ion coverage of 81.4% versus 44.9% for decoys. None of these lists is deposited. I also could not open the 10 TIFF supplementary figures (no image reader available here), so everything that exists only as a figure - the per-sample peptide counts in Fig. 3A, the de novo tag overlaps in Fig. S1A, the database-size comparison in Fig. S3A, the three-tier filtering waterfall in Fig. 6E, the recurrent-antigen heatmap in Fig. 6H - is paper-claim-only for me. I never ran the TIPs pipeline and never reproduced any identification.

a1_downloadable.note: FAILS. Nothing is behind a login and no link is dead, so this is not an access-application failure - it is a 'the result was never deposited' failure. The paper's product is a list of roughly 2,700 transposable-element-derived peptides presented on HLA class I molecules (cell-surface proteins that display peptide fragments to T cells). I searched every artefact: the Zenodo record is one 309,585-byte code zip, the GitHub tree has 60 code files and no data directory, and the only data file in the article is a 30,089-byte Word document holding 30 unique peptides. The Data availability statement lists only the three input PRIDE accessions and the three input GEO series; it names no deposit for the paper's own output. Those inputs are 480+ gigabytes of raw Thermo .raw mass-spectrometry files, which my own project rules forbid downloading and which a laptop cannot process.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAILS, and this is the cleanest kill. Any sensible target here - 'is this transposable-element-encoded peptide actually presented on HLA class I?' - exists as a column in no downloadable file. To build it you would have to re-run the entire four-step TIPs pipeline: translate transposable-element-annotated regions of the human genome in all six reading frames (bedtools plus seqkit against Dfam release 3.9), run three deep-learning de novo sequencing models (Casanovo, InstaNovo, PepNet) over every tandem mass spectrum, map tags back with blastp-short at 100% identity, then search with three engines (MSFragger, MS-GF+, Comet), rescore with PeptideProphet, integrate with iProphet and apply a grouped 3% false discovery rate. That is 16 tools, listed in the paper's own Table S4, standing between raw data and a label.

a3_inputs_present.note: Passes only for the 30 peptides that are deposited: their amino-acid sequences are literally in the table, so no identifier lookup is needed. But the candidate space - the 'inflated' transposable-element protein database that defines what could have been presented, and therefore defines the negatives - is not deposited either and would have to be rebuilt from the human genome plus Dfam release 3.9. So the inputs for the 30 positives are present; the inputs for every negative are not.

a4_units_stated.note: Passes, and this is the paper's best data-quality feature. I read the headers myself: 'Probability' is a unitless 0-1 posterior from iProphet, 'Spectral Count' is an integer number of matching spectra, 'Best Allele Rank (%)' is a percentile explicitly in percent, 'Charge state' is an integer, and Table S4 states every tool version and threshold (20 parts per million mass tolerance, peptide length 8-15, 3% false discovery rate, binder cut-off under 2%). No blank cells in any of the four tables.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAILS by two orders of magnitude. I counted 30 unique peptide sequences in the only data file (9 in Table S2, 21 in Table S3), across 34 table rows, from 13 samples. The checklist needs about 400 rows for classification and 1,500 for regression. Worse, 21 of the 30 peptides come from a single glioblastoma cell line (LNT-229), and all 30 are positives - there is not one negative example in the paper.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: What is deposited: 13 MB of supplementary Word files and 310 KB of code, which is trivial. What the paper's own task needs: 480+ gigabytes of raw mass spectrometry, which I summed myself from the PRIDE application programming interface (PXD003790 = 172,542,596,998 bytes across 65 files; PXD013649 = 84,018,210,451 bytes across 97 files; PXD034772 = 229,776,196,927 bytes on the first page of 100 files alone), plus a six-frame translation of every transposable-element-annotated region of the human genome.
a6_fits_laptop.note: FAILS for the paper's task, trivially passes for what is deposited - and that gap is the whole problem. Running three deep-learning de novo sequencing models over millions of tandem mass spectra needs a graphics card; searching an inflated transposable-element database with MSFragger routinely needs 32 GB or more of memory. My project rules also explicitly forbid downloading raw mass-spectrometry files, so I recorded sizes only.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: FAILS, though mostly for lack of anything to check against: no file contains any of the paper's headline counts. Where I could check, I found two real discrepancies. (1) The text says 'eight peptides derived from [LINE] ORFs ... six peptides from four distinct regions of the ORF2 protein, along with two peptides from two sites in ORF1', but Table S2 contains 7 unique LINE peptide sequences in 8 rows - 5 unique from ORF2, not 6 - because IVSAQNLIK is listed twice for two different samples. The paper is counting sample-peptide pairs as 'peptides'. (2) The text reports 26 distinct endogenous-retrovirus peptides; Table S2 lists 2. Separately, Table S1 lists 13 samples while Figure 2 describes 'five tumor or cell line samples' and Figure 6 covers 12, with no file saying which 13, 12 or 5 were used where.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAILS, and in the textbook circular way. Every candidate label column in this paper is another model's output. 'Probability' is an iProphet posterior, downstream of PeptideProphet rescoring of three search engines, whose candidate database was itself built from the predictions of three deep-learning de novo sequencers. 'Best Allele Rank (%)' is a MixMHCpred version 3.0 prediction - so training anything on 'is this a binder' would be distilling MixMHCpred, and the paper's own 83.4%-binder headline is a model agreeing with a model. The paper's one genuine physical anchor is small and honest: synthetic peptide standards were run on the mass spectrometer for the 8-ish LINE and LTR peptides in Table S2 and some SVA peptides (Figures S7, S8), which I could not open. So about 9 peptides have a real measurement behind them and the remaining roughly 2,700 claimed identifications have a model chain behind them.

existing_models.name: TIPs itself (the paper's pipeline: three deep-learning de novo sequencers feeding three database search engines, with grouped false-discovery-rate control)
existing_models.score_and_split: Code is MIT-licensed on GitHub and archived on Zenodo, both of which I listed and confirmed are code-only. The reported result is a 20-fold average increase in transposable-element-derived peptides over NewAnce at the same 3% false discovery rate, with 83.4% of its peptides called binders by MixMHCpred versus NewAnce's 83.3%. There is no train/test split because it is a search pipeline, not a trained predictor - which also means there is no held-out number to beat. All figures read from the paper text, not reproduced.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The Discussion has no limitations section, but it names two open problems: high sequence identity between transposable-element copies 'complicates the attribution of their origin' (25.4% of peptides map to several genomic loci), and the mechanism producing peptides from regions 'conventionally considered non-coding' is unexplained - they speculate about promoter-independent translation. They also flag extension to circular-RNA and long-non-coding-RNA peptides as future work.

existing_models.name: NewAnce (Chong et al. 2020, Nature Communications, the direct comparator for non-canonical immunopeptidomics)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported by the TIPs authors as finding 11 transposable-element peptides in sample 0D5P, of which only 2 were confirmed with synthetic peptide standards, and 24 in sample T1185B. TIPs reports recovering both validated ones plus 187 more. I retrieved the Nature Communications landing page in search results and read its summary (it intersects MaxQuant and Comet peptide-spectrum matches with group-specific false-discovery-rate control) but I did not retrieve the paper itself or verify whether its code is installable. Its source mass-spectrometry deposit PXD013649 does contain eight 'search_*.zip' result bundles of 23-60 MB plus a 954,495,630-byte paper_data.zip, which I listed but did not download.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not retrieved - I did not open the primary paper.

existing_models.name: Casanovo v2, InstaNovo v1.0.0 and PepNet v2.0 (three open deep-learning models that read an amino-acid sequence directly off a tandem mass spectrum)
existing_models.score_and_split: These are the actual pretrained models inside TIPs, named with versions in the paper's Table S4, which I read. TIPs reports no accuracy number for any of them individually; it only applies a quality filter (per-residue confidence at least 0.75, tag length at least 8 amino acids) and takes the union of their outputs. Their own published benchmarks were not retrieved by me.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: The TIPs authors state explicitly that de novo outputs 'do not by themselves determine peptide origin or ensure TE derivation' - i.e. the tags are too unreliable to be trusted alone, which is exactly why TIPs wraps them in a database search.

existing_models.name: MixMHCpred v3.0 and DeepLC v3.1.8 (a peptide-HLA binding predictor and a chromatography retention-time predictor, both used by the paper as 'orthogonal validation')
existing_models.score_and_split: Used, not benchmarked, in this paper. MixMHCpred produced the 83.4% binder figure and the 'Best Allele Rank (%)' column I read in Tables S2 and S3; DeepLC produced the r = 0.94 hydrophobicity-versus-retention-time correlation. Both numbers are from the paper text. These matter for scoring because they are the source of the only quantitative columns in the deposited tables, which makes those columns unusable as training labels.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Supplementary Note 2 argues these predictors are 'extensively benchmarked and widely recognized for their robust performance', so the authors treat them as solved rather than naming a gap.

existing_models.name: The crowded HLA-presentation prediction field: ImmuneApp (Nature Communications 2024), MARIA, MUNIS, NeoMHCI, and a geometric-deep-learning MHC-peptide method
existing_models.score_and_split: I found these in two web searches and read only the result titles and snippets, so treat every figure as unverified: NeoMHCI is summarised as reaching an area under the receiver-operating-characteristic curve of 0.948 on unseen multi-allele ligand presentation, and MUNIS as trained on 651,237 unique HLA class I ligands. The point for this evaluation is the scale: open models in this field are trained on hundreds of thousands of ligands, against which 30 deposited peptides is not a dataset.

existing_models.name: pXg (Molecular and Cellular Proteomics 2024) and dbPepNeo2.0 (a curated neoantigen peptide database)
existing_models.score_and_split: Adjacent, and relevant as possible label sources rather than competitors. pXg is summarised in search results as identifying non-canonical MHC class I peptides from de novo sequencing combined with RNA-sequencing reads - the same problem TIPs attacks. dbPepNeo2.0 is described as adding non-coding-region neoantigens and offering bulk download. I retrieved neither resource and verified no count in either.

backbone.name: ESM-2 (a protein language model with small open checkpoints that run on a laptop processor) would be the obvious thing to freeze and fit a head to, encoding each 8-15 amino-acid peptide plus its HLA allele sequence. A peptide-HLA-specific alternative would be a transformer trained on binding data such as TransPHLA. Notably the paper uses no learned representation at all for the peptides themselves - its deep learning is confined to reading sequences off spectra.
backbone.hardware: Technically yes on this laptop: embedding 30 peptides with ESM-2's 35-million-parameter checkpoint takes seconds on a processor, and even 100,000 peptides would be a couple of hours. The backbone is not the problem; there is nothing to train it on. Reproducing the paper's own pipeline would need a graphics card for the three de novo sequencers and 32 GB or more for MSFragger against an inflated database.
backbone.licence: ESM-2 weights are openly downloadable (MIT). TIPs code is MIT, both on GitHub and Zenodo. The article itself is CC BY-NC-ND, which is non-commercial and forbids derivatives of the text (not of the data). Two of the three input mass-spectrometry deposits are CC0; PXD003790 is under 'EBI terms of use'.

integration.partner_dataset: Dfam release 3.9, the open transposable-element family database the paper itself used, which carries consensus sequences, copy numbers and estimated insertion ages for every subfamily. Second: the HLA Ligand Atlas and dbPepNeo2.0 (curated catalogues of peptides observed on HLA molecules), joinable directly on the amino-acid sequence. Third: UniProt, because Table S2's 'Target Protein' column already uses UniProt entry names (LORF1_HUMAN, LORF2_HUMAN).
integration.join_key: Transposable-element subfamily name (L1HS, L1PA3, SVA_D, HERVS71-int, ERVL-B4-int - all present and all standard Dfam identifiers), the bare peptide amino-acid sequence, four-digit HLA allele codes in Table S1, and UniProt entry names for the two LINE open-reading-frame proteins. The identifiers are genuinely good; there is just almost nothing attached to them.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Can you predict, from a transposable-element subfamily's consensus sequence, copy number and evolutionary age alone, how many HLA-presented peptides it will contribute across tumours - which would let you rank the roughly 1,500 human subfamilies for antigen potential without running mass spectrometry? That question is well posed and the paper's own r = 0.72 copy-number correlation says there is signal, but answering it needs per-subfamily peptide counts for many samples, and the deposited files give you 5 SVA subfamilies in one cell line and 7 LINE/LTR subfamilies in five others.

controls.positive_control: Good ones exist and two are already published, which is the frustrating part: a working pipeline must recover the r = 0.72 correlation between a subfamily's genomic copy number and the number of peptides it yields, and the r = 0.94 correlation between DeepLC-predicted hydrophobicity and observed chromatographic retention time. A third, cheaper one: any model of HLA class I presentation must put 9-mers at the top, since 9 amino acids is the textbook dominant length and Figure S2H reports exactly that enrichment.
controls.negative_control: Decoy peptides are already built into the pipeline (sequence-reversed database entries), and the paper reports the right contrast: 81.4% fragment-ion coverage for real peptides versus 44.9% for decoys. For any model I built on the deposited rows, label shuffling would be meaningless at n = 30. The untested negative control that matters is the circularity one: strip the MixMHCpred and iProphet columns and check whether anything predictive remains.
controls.external_validation: Two plausible sources, neither opened by me. First, the NewAnce transposable-element peptide list from Chong et al. 2020, whose result bundles sit in PRIDE PXD013649 as eight zips of 23-60 MB - small enough to download, and the honest cross-check of TIPs' 20-fold claim. Second, the 45 spectra-validated treatment-induced endogenous-retrovirus neopeptides reported in a 2023 Nature Communications paper on DNA-methyltransferase and histone-deacetylase inhibition, which I found in search but did not retrieve. There is no year or source column in any deposited table, so the cheap temporal split is unavailable.

honest_claim_h3: With what is actually downloadable, the most anyone could honestly claim is: 'among 30 transposable-element-derived peptides that three search engines agreed on and that MixMHCpred already calls strong HLA binders, 21 of which come from one decitabine-treated glioblastoma cell line, a model can reproduce MixMHCpred's own binding rank' - which is a claim about MixMHCpred, not about antigen presentation, and rests on no negative examples at all.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a short peptide's amino-acid sequence and the patient's immune-presenting genes to predict whether a jumping-gene peptide reaches the cell surface.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example would be one 8-to-15-amino-acid peptide encoded by a transposable element (a 'jumping gene' - repeated DNA that copies itself around the genome and makes up about half of human DNA), paired with the HLA type of the sample it came from. The paper implies roughly 2,700 such peptides exist in its results, but I verified only 30 unique peptide sequences are deposited anywhere, so the usable count is 30, not 2,700.
plain_idea.predict: A probability that the peptide is displayed on the cell surface by HLA class I molecules, which are the proteins that show peptide fragments to killer T cells. The true answer is supposed to come from mass spectrometry of peptides stripped off real tumour cells - but in the deposited tables the only numeric columns are themselves software outputs (an iProphet confidence score and a MixMHCpred binding rank), with real synthetic-peptide confirmation for only about 9 peptides.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Cancer immunotherapy groups hunting 'off-the-shelf' tumour targets would use it, because transposable-element peptides can be shared across patients in a way that mutation-derived neoantigens are not, and because the drug decitabine seems to switch them on. Even a failed model would tell us whether presentation of these peptides is predictable from sequence or is dominated by where in the genome the element sits.

ml_idea: Three framings, all dead for the same reason - the paper's output was never deposited. (1) Train a presentation predictor on the TIPs peptides. There are 30 unique peptides in the only data file I could open (9 in Table S2, 21 in Table S3), all positives, 21 of them from a single cell line, against a field whose open models train on hundreds of thousands of ligands. (2) Reproduce or improve the pipeline. That means 480+ gigabytes of raw Thermo .raw files whose sizes I summed from the PRIDE application programming interface, three graphics-card-hungry de novo sequencing models, and a six-frame translation of every transposable-element region of the human genome - squarely outside a 16 GB laptop and outside my own rule against downloading raw mass spectrometry. (3) Model the subfamily-level question instead: predict how many presented peptides a transposable-element subfamily yields from its consensus sequence, copy number and age. This is the one genuinely interesting idea here, it joins cleanly to Dfam release 3.9 on subfamily name, and the paper's own r = 0.72 says there is signal - but the per-subfamily counts live only in Figure 3A and Figure S6F as bar charts, so the label is a picture, not a column. What is salvageable is a short, specific note rather than a project, built on three things I verified in the files and the paper has not stated: the text's 'eight LINE ORF peptides' is 7 unique sequences in 8 rows because IVSAQNLIK is double-counted across two samples, and 'six ORF2 peptides' is 5 unique sequences; 26 endogenous-retrovirus peptides are claimed but 2 are listed; and Table S1 assigns cell lines T98G and LNT-229 implausible HLA types (A*02:917 homozygous, B*39:187 homozygous, C*04:274), which look like transcription errors in the very column that drives every MixMHCpred binding call in the paper. Asking the authors to deposit the peptide table would be worth more than any model I could fit on 30 rows.

effort.compute_note: Two sets of numbers, and the gap between them is the verdict. The figures above describe only what is deposited: 13 MB of Word files that my own parser read in under a second, 30 peptides that ESM-2's small checkpoint would embed in seconds, and a cross-validation run that is instant at n = 30 and statistically meaningless. The paper's own task is a different universe: 480+ gigabytes of raw mass spectrometry (sizes summed by me from the PRIDE application programming interface, nothing downloaded), three deep-learning de novo sequencers that need a graphics card, and MSFragger against an inflated six-frame transposable-element database that typically wants 32 GB or more - hence needs_gpu true. Nothing was timed on a model; I ran no training. Measured timings: the full-text XML arrived instantly, the 8,024,429-byte supplementary bundle took about 100 seconds, and the Zenodo, GitHub and PRIDE application programming interface calls were all sub-second.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Open Additional file 2 (13059_2026_4191_MOESM2_ESM.docx, 30,089 bytes) and count the peptide rows. Two minutes, and it kills the project: Tables S2 and S3 hold 34 rows and 30 unique peptide sequences, 21 of them from one cell line, where the paper implies about 2,700 peptides exist. Second-cheapest, three more minutes: list the Zenodo record (one 309,585-byte code zip) and the GitHub tree (60 files, all code, no data directory) to confirm the full list is deposited nowhere. Do both before reading the Methods.

verdict_reason: Fails Part A at A1, A2, A5, A6, A7 and A8 - all six checked in the files, not inferred from the abstract. The kill is A1 plus A5 together: the paper's product is a catalogue of roughly 2,700 transposable-element-derived HLA class I peptides, and that catalogue is deposited nowhere. I listed every artefact myself. The Zenodo record 10.5281/zenodo.18595612 is a single 309,585-byte code zip. The GitHub tree (WgShaoLab/TIPs, MIT, 60 entries, not truncated) is pipeline code with no data directory. The Data availability statement names only the three input PRIDE deposits and three input GEO series - nothing for the paper's own output. The one data file in the whole article is a 30,089-byte Word document, and my own table parser found exactly 13 sample rows, 11 peptide rows in Table S2 (9 unique sequences, 7 LINE and 2 LTR) and 23 peptide rows in Table S3 (21 unique sequences, every one from the single cell line LNT-229): 30 unique peptides total, all positives, no negative examples anywhere. A2 compounds it - rebuilding the label means re-running all 16 tools in the paper's own Table S4 over 480+ gigabytes of raw Thermo .raw files, whose sizes I summed from the PRIDE application programming interface (172.5 GB, 84.0 GB and 229.8 GB for the three accessions), which my rules forbid downloading and which needs a graphics card and 32 GB of memory (A6). A8 is the subtle one and it is a clean circularity failure: the only two numeric columns in the deposited tables are an iProphet posterior probability and a MixMHCpred binding rank, both software outputs, so training on either distils an existing predictor rather than learning biology - and the paper's own 83.4%-binder headline is one model agreeing with another. Real synthetic-peptide confirmation exists for only about 9 peptides. A7 fails too, and here I can be concrete: the text's 'eight peptides from LINE open reading frames' is 7 unique sequences in 8 rows (IVSAQNLIK is listed twice for two samples) and its 'six ORF2 peptides' is 5 unique sequences; 26 endogenous-retrovirus peptides are claimed and 2 are listed; Table S1 gives 13 samples while Figure 2 describes 5 and Figure 6 covers 12. Three things are genuinely good and none rescue it: the identifiers are clean and standard (Dfam subfamily names, UniProt entry names, four-digit HLA codes), every column has stated units with zero blank cells, and the code is MIT-licensed. One further file-level observation worth sending to the authors: Table S1 assigns the glioblastoma lines T98G and LNT-229 implausible HLA types (A*02:917 and B*39:187 homozygous, C*04:274), and those alleles are the input to every binding call in the paper.
